title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
description: Why doing well with money has less to do with how smart you are and more to do with how you behave. Every chapter, distilled into a 5-minute episode with a full transcript.

episodes.title: No One’s Crazy
episodes.summary: Your money habits come from your own experiences, which is why everyone’s choices make sense to them.

transcript.text: People do some crazy things with money. But no one is actually crazy.
Each of us has a different set of experiences that shapes how the world works.
Someone who grew up during high inflation sees risk very differently from someone who didn’t.
What you lived through counts for more than what you read about.
That is why two smart people can look at the same market and disagree.
Retirement saving, index funds and credit cards are all newer than they feel.
We are all still new to this, and learning as we go.
So the next decision that looks crazy probably makes sense to the person making it.
Takeaway: start from empathy. Everyone is working from their own story.

takeaways: Your money habits come from your own experiences, which is why everyone’s choices make sense to them.
Look for where this already shows up in your own decisions.
Pick one small change and keep it going long enough to compound.

episodes.title: Confounding Compounding
episodes.summary: Modest returns held for a very long time beat big returns you can’t sustain.

transcript.text: Compounding is easy to explain and hard to feel. Our instincts expect growth in straight lines.
But growth that builds on itself curves upward, and most of the curve shows up late.
In a long investing life, the biggest gains usually arrive in the final decades, not the first.
That makes time the variable people underrate the most.
Many investors chase the highest possible return. This chapter argues for a different target.
Aim for good returns you can stay with, through downturns, boredom and the urge to tinker.
Quitting early is the most expensive mistake, because it resets the clock compounding depends on.
The same idea reaches beyond money. Skills, relationships and reputation compound too.
Takeaway: protect the streak. Staying in the game is the strategy.

takeaways: Compounding rewards time far more than it rewards a high rate of return.
Choose returns you can sustain for decades over returns you can’t live with.
Avoid moves that interrupt the process. Staying invested is the edge.
